text:
Most people over 60 were told to avoid eggs. After nearly 40 years in medicine, Dr. Henry Jason looked at what the research actually says, and one effect shows up within weeks that almost nobody expects. 🥚

In this video, you’ll learn what happens when eggs become a regular part of your life after 60, organ by organ and system by system. We cover how eggs may support muscle strength and help fight sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss), why the protein, choline, vitamin B12, and folate in eggs matter for brain health and memory, and how the lutein and zeaxanthin in egg yolks may help protect your eyes from macular degeneration and cataracts. We also look at vitamin D, vitamin K2, bone health, steady energy and blood sugar, and sleep.

Then comes the honest part: what eating four eggs a day really means for your cholesterol, who may be a hyper-responder, how many eggs per day is reasonable for seniors, the safest way to cook eggs, and which health conditions mean you should talk to your own doctor first, including diabetes, heart disease, high LDL, and kidney disease.

If you’re over 60 and wondering whether eggs are good or bad for you, this is a clear, practical, research-based guide to protecting your strength, memory, vision, and independence as you age.

📚 SOURCES AND RESEARCH REFERENCED

CDC: data on falls among adults 65+
Dietary Guidelines for Americans (2015): removal of the strict daily dietary cholesterol limit
BMJ systematic review and meta-analysis (Rong et al., 2013): egg intake and heart disease/stroke risk
JAMA (Zhong et al., 2019): dietary cholesterol, egg consumption, and cardiovascular risk
Framingham Offspring Study (Poly et al., 2011): choline intake and cognitive performance
University of Connecticut study (Goodrow et al., 2006): one egg daily in older adults and blood lutein/zeaxanthin
van Vliet et al., 2017: whole eggs vs. egg whites and muscle protein synthesis in young men
Vander Wal et al., 2005: egg breakfast vs. bagel breakfast and satiety
Observational research on lutein/zeaxanthin intake and advanced macular degeneration (including AREDS2)

Disclaimer: This video is for educational purposes only and is not a substitute for professional medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. The benefits discussed are not guaranteed, and individual nutritional needs vary. Consult a qualified healthcare professional about your personal health and dietary needs.

👍 Like, subscribe, and tell me in the comments how you like your eggs.

#SeniorHealth #EggsAfter60 #HealthyAging #Over60 #Nutrition

text:
Doctors notice these 9 hygiene mistakes after 65 almost immediately, and most people can't smell them on themselves. In this video, Dr. Henry Jason explains what causes "old person smell," why it becomes more common with age, and the simple changes that can help, starting tonight.

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN
Why smell changes with age, and why deodorant alone doesn't fix it
How to make bathing safer if you're afraid of falling
Where moisture and odor hide (skin folds, feet, pillowcases, towels)
Simple tools for mouth, scalp and bathroom care
When a change in smell is a reason to call your doctor

If you're helping someone you love, the video also covers how to raise this topic gently and privately.

If this video helped you, please like, subscribe, and share it with someone you love.

text:
Blurry vision after 60 doesn't have one cause. It has at least five. Some are harmless and fixable in an afternoon, and one of them is painless and can quietly take away your central vision while you blame the restaurant lighting. In this video, retired doctor Henry Jason walks through the 5 real causes of blurry vision after 60, from presbyopia and dry eye to cataracts and macular degeneration, plus what actually slows the decline.

👁️ In this video:
5 causes of blurry vision after 60, ranked from common to serious
The warning signs of cataracts, macular degeneration, and glaucoma
Vision changes that are emergencies and need same-day care
Why a dilated eye exam matters (and how often to get one)
How to use an Amsler grid at home
Lifestyle habits linked to lower risk of eye disease
The truth about eye vitamins (AREDS2)

text:
What really happens to your body during a stroke? In this video you'll learn three things most people never hear: a stroke usually doesn't hurt, the damage keeps spreading while you feel fine, and your own brain can hide the stroke from you. Plus the one simple sentence that can get past "I'm fine" and save minutes that matter.

Learn the early stroke warning signs and symptoms, the difference between an ischemic stroke, a hemorrhagic stroke and a mini-stroke (TIA), how BE FAST works, and exactly what to do if someone you love may be having a stroke. We also cover what the emergency team does, stroke treatment (clot-busting medicine and thrombectomy), the aspirin myth, and stroke recovery and brain rewiring (neuroplasticity).

Stroke risk goes up with age, especially after 55. High blood pressure and atrial fibrillation (AFib) are two of the biggest risk factors, so we finish with three questions to ask your doctor and a 10-minute homework plan for you and your family.

TIMESTAMPS

0:00 Margaret's 58 minutes
1:53 Does a stroke hurt?
3:02 Thing 1: A stroke usually doesn't hurt
3:27 Ischemic stroke, hemorrhagic stroke and mini-stroke (TIA)
4:54 Thing 2: The damage keeps spreading (time is brain)
6:12 Thing 3: Your brain can hide the stroke from you
7:46 What happens when you call 911
10:04 3 myths: aspirin, "it went away," "wait and see"
11:44 Bonus: the sentence that gets past "I'm fine"
12:18 BE FAST stroke signs
13:37 Recovery and hidden risks
15:22 Risk factors and questions for your doctor
16:23 Back to the kitchen
📚 Research & Sources Referenced

CDC — Stroke Facts and Statistics
American Heart Association / American Stroke Association — 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke
Stroke (AHA journal) — "Time Is Brain—Quantified," 2006
Stroke (AHA journal) — AHA Scientific Statement on Transient Ischemic Attack (Mini-Stroke), 2023
Stroke (AHA journal) — Poststroke Depression Scientific Statement, 2017
American Heart Association — Atrial Fibrillation and Stroke Risk
New England Journal of Medicine — DAWN and DEFUSE 3 Thrombectomy Trials, 2018
Annals of Emergency Medicine — Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale, 1999
NINDS (NIH) — Know Stroke Campaign and BE FAST
American Heart Association — Heart Disease and Stroke Statistics

Medical Disclaimer: This video is for educational and health-awareness purposes only and is not a substitute for personalized medical advice. Anesthesia and surgery decisions should always be discussed with your surgeon and anesthesiologist, who can assess your individual health history, medications, and risks.

Margaret and Walter's story is a composite built from what stroke survivors and their families describe. This video is for educational purposes only. It is not medical advice and never replaces emergency care. If you think someone is having a stroke, call your local emergency number immediately (911 in the United States). Do not start, stop, or change any medication because of this video; talk to your own doctor.

#Stroke #BEFAST #SeniorHealth #StrokeSymptoms

text:
She's 103 and eats red potatoes, whole eggs, ground beef, and olive oil every day. Here's what the research says about each food, the caution for your kidneys or heart, and the mistake almost everyone makes with olive oil. A senior nutrition countdown for adults over 60.

Muscle loss (sarcopenia), falls, and frailty are real risks after 60, and food is one of the tools you can use. In this video, Dr. Henry Jason breaks down four foods many seniors fear: how much to eat, how to prepare them, who should be careful, and what to ask your own doctor.

Note: Diana is a made-up illustrative character used to organize this video. The evidence comes from the studies listed below, not from her.

⏱ TIMESTAMPS
0:30 Sarcopenia (muscle loss) and falls in older adults
0:55 Ultra-processed food and frailty
1:22 The four foods + Diana's morning habit
1:51 About this video and disclaimer
2:28 #4 Red potatoes: potassium, resistant starch, kidney and medication cautions
5:32 #3 Whole eggs: protein, choline, and the cholesterol debate
8:40 #2 Ground beef: B12, iron, zinc, and how much is too much
12:03 Why hasn't your doctor told you this?
12:58 Diana's morning habit (sit-to-stand exercise)
13:43 #1 Olive oil: the evidence, and the 3 mistakes
17:51 Your action plan + 4 questions to ask your doctor
18:31 Final thoughts

📚 SOURCES REFERENCED
Drouin-Chartier JP et al. Egg consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease (three US cohorts, systematic review and meta-analysis). BMJ, 2020
Zhong VW et al. Associations of dietary cholesterol or egg consumption with incident cardiovascular disease and mortality. JAMA, 2019
Estruch R et al. Primary prevention of cardiovascular disease with a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil or nuts (PREDIMED). New England Journal of Medicine, republished 2018
Guasch-Ferré M et al. Consumption of olive oil and risk of total and cause-specific mortality among U.S. adults. Journal of the American College of Cardiology, 2022

PROT-AGE Study Group and ESPEN guidance on protein intake for older adults (about 1.0 to 1.2 g per kg body weight)
CDC data on falls among adults 65 and older
Observational research on ultra-processed food intake and frailty in older adults

text:
4 Real Reasons Why Aging Suddenly Speeds Up After 75 (And The One Thing That Slows It Back Down)

Why does the body seem to change so fast after 75? It's not random, and it's not "just getting old." In this video, I break down the real science behind why aging after 75 feels different — the immune system changes, cellular aging, and chronic inflammation that quietly build up for decades before suddenly showing up all at once. Then I walk through the one research-backed thing — resistance training for seniors — that genuinely helps push back against it, with a simple 7-day and 4-week plan you can start today.

If you've noticed slower recovery after 75, muscle loss in old age, or unexplained fatigue in your 70s, this video explains the actual mechanism behind it — the Cleanup Gap — and what you can realistically do about it.

⏱️ WHAT YOU'LL LEARN 
00:00 Why aging suddenly speeds up after 75 
01:33 Why this channel exists 02:15 The Cleanup Gap explained 02:39 Reason 1: Immune aging (immunosenescence) 
03:53 Reason 2: Senescent "zombie" cells

06:50 Reason 4: Chronic inflammation (inflammaging)
